title: What does `Stream.of(1,2,3).map(i -> i * 2)` return if no terminal operation is called? (Nothing — streams are lazy.)
shortTitle: What does Stream.of(1,2,3).map(i -> i * 2) return if no terminal operation is called?

s1_definition.profdef: Intermediate operations like `map` are lazy — they only build a pipeline description and do not execute. Without a terminal operation nothing runs, so the mapping function is never applied and no values are produced.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya sets up the conveyor belt and the doubling machine, but until someone presses the start button at the end, nothing moves and nothing is doubled.
s1_definition.oneliner: Intermediate ops are lazy — no terminal operation means `map` never executes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Intermediate operations like `map` are lazy — they only build a pipeline description and do not execute. Without a terminal operation nothing runs, so the mapping function is never applied and no values are produced.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya sets up the conveyor belt and the doubling machine, but until someone presses the start button at the end, nothing moves and nothing is doubled.

**One line to remember:** Intermediate ops are lazy — no terminal operation means `map` never executes.

sections.s2_technical:
`Stream.of(1, 2, 3).map(i -> i * 2)` returns a `Stream<Integer>` object representing the pipeline, but the map function has not run. Intermediate operations are lazy: they record what to do and return a new stream, deferring all work until a terminal operation like `collect`, `forEach`, `count`, or `reduce` pulls elements through.

So with no terminal, you hold a configured but un-executed stream; the doubling never happens and no output exists. Adding a terminal, for example `.collect(toList())`, triggers execution and produces two, four, six.

The senior nuance is that laziness enables important optimisations: operations fuse so each element flows through the whole pipeline once, and short-circuiting terminals like `findFirst` or `limit` stop early without processing the rest. A pipeline that ends at an intermediate operation is a no-op and usually a bug — a forgotten terminal. Understanding laziness explains why `peek` with no terminal prints nothing and why ordering of work is element-by-element.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at the National Bank of India wrote a stream that mapped amounts but forgot the terminal, and wondered why nothing happened.

This is exactly stream laziness — the demo shows the pipeline doing nothing until a terminal is added.

The code shows a no-terminal pipeline versus a terminal one in a `LazyService.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/lazy/LazyDemo.java
java -cp out com.bank.lazy.LazyDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Step 1: The no-terminal method builds a stream with a map that prints and doubles.

Step 2: Because there is no terminal, the map lambda is never invoked, so nothing is printed from it — the pipeline just sits there.

Step 3: The with-terminal method adds toList, which pulls the elements through.

Step 4: Now map runs, doubling one, two, three into two, four, six.

```
with terminal: [2, 4, 6]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Stream.of(1,2,3).map(x2)        ← no terminal → NOTHING runs (lazy)
     returns a configured Stream, map never applied

  Stream.of(1,2,3).map(x2).toList()  ← terminal → runs → [2, 4, 6]
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Stream Laziness ═══

  intermediate ops (map/filter) = recorded, not run
  terminal op (collect/forEach/count) = triggers execution
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — lazy evaluation ═══

  ┌─ build vs execute ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ map/filter: LAZY → build pipeline, return new Stream        │
  │ no terminal → nothing executes (map never applied)          │
  │ terminal (collect/forEach/count/reduce) → pulls elements     │
  │ laziness enables fusion (one pass) + short-circuit (limit)   │
  │ pipeline ending at intermediate op = no-op (usually a bug)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │             LazyService       │
  │  + noTerminal(): void             │ map never runs
  │  + withTerminal(): List            │ toList triggers map
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. Stream.of(...).map(...)  → lazy, nothing runs
  2. + toList()               → terminal, now runs
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Stream of one, two, three dot map returns a Stream object that represents the pipeline, but the map function has not run — intermediate operations are lazy. map simply records what to do and returns a new stream, deferring all work until a terminal operation like collect, forEach, count, or reduce pulls the elements through. So with no terminal, the doubling never happens and no output is produced; I just hold a configured but un-executed stream.

At the National Bank of India a developer hit exactly this — a stream that mapped amounts but had no terminal, so nothing happened and they could not see why. Adding a terminal such as toList immediately triggers execution and yields two, four, six.

The senior point I stress is that this laziness is not a quirk but a deliberate design that enables key optimisations: operations fuse so each element flows through the whole pipeline in a single pass, and short-circuiting terminals like findFirst or limit stop early without touching the rest. A pipeline that ends at an intermediate operation is a no-op and almost always a bug — a forgotten terminal — and the same laziness is why peek prints nothing without a terminal.
